documentNotes.title: Native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface
Preface
Preface
Preface 
This publication contains the competition problems (Volume 2) from the 21st – 40th 
International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 1989 – 2008  and is a 
continuation of the publication that appeared last year as Volume 1 and contained 
competition problems from the first twenty IChOs.  The whole review of the competition 
tasks set in the IChO in its fourty-year history is a contribution of the IChO International 
Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) to the development of this world known 
international competition. This Volume 2 contains 154 theoretical and 46 practical 
competition problems from the mentioned years. The review as a whole presents 
altogether 279 theoretical and 96 practical problems.  
In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because 
the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form 
that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was 
necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems. However, 
they did not concern the contents and language of the problems.  
Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and 
due to the procedure of the creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to 
assign any author's name to a particular problem. As the editor I would appreciate many  
times some discussion with the authors about any critical places that occurred in the text. 
On the other hand, any additional amendments to the text would be not correct from the  
historical point of view. Therefore, responsibility for the scientific content and language of 
the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry 
Olympiads.    
 
Some parts of texts, especially those gained as scanned materials, could not be 
used directly and thus, several texts, schemes and pictures had to be re-written or created 
again. Some solutions were often available in a brief form and necessary extent only, just 
for the needs of members of the International Jury.  
 
Recalculations of the solutions were made in some special cases only when the 
numeric results in the original solutions showed to be obviously not correct. Although the 
numbers of significant figures in the results of several solutions do not obey the criteria 
generally accepted, they were left without change.      


 
In this publication SI quantities and units are used and a more modern method of 
chemical calculations is introduced. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an 
effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI.  
There were some problems with the presentation of the solutions of practical tasks, 
because most of the relatively simple calculations were based on the experimental results 
of contestants. Moreover, the practical problems are accompanied with answer sheets in 
the last years and several additional questions and tasks have appeared in them that were 
not a part of the text of the original experimental problems. Naturally, answer sheets could 
not be included in this publication and can only be preserved as archive materials. 
  
When reading the texts of the IChO problems one must admire and appreciate the 
work of those many known and unknown people – teachers, authors, pupils, and 
organizers – who contributed so much to development and success of this important 
international competition. 
 
I am sure about the usefulness of the this review of the IChO problems. It may serve 
not only as archive material but, in particular, this review should serve to both competitors 
and their teachers as a source of further inspiration in their preparation for this challenging 
competition. 
 
 
 
 
Bratislava, July 2009  
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
                                    Anton Sirota, editor

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.statement:
Chemists at Merck Frosst Canada in Montréal have developed a promising drug which is useful against asthma. The structure of MK-0476 is shown below.

![](p3-fig1)

During their investigation, they devised a simple and efficient synthesis, depicted below, for the thiolated portion of MK-0476 starting from diethyl ester **A**.

![](p3-fig2)

parts.statement:
Give the structures of the intermediate products **B–F** prepared during this synthesis.

In one of the last steps of the synthesis on MK-0476, the dilithium salt of the above thiol acid (**G**) was coupled with the side chain of the rest of the molecule as shown below.

![](p3-fig3)
Based on the observed stereochemistry of the above reaction, what is the mechanistic designation of this coupling process?

If the process proceeds by your proposed mechanism, what change would occur to the overall rate of the reaction if the concentration of both the thiolate salt and the substrate **H** were simultaneously tripled?

For the nucleophilic substitution reaction, model studies were carried out using bromoethane as the substrate to perfect the above coupling. Draw only the structure of the major product of the reaction of one molar equivalent of bromoethane with:

a) **G** plus two molar equivalents of base.

b) **G** plus one molar equivalent of base.
A side reaction of **G** is its oxidative dimerization. Draw the structure of the dimeric product, showing all non-bonded electrons.

sections.statement: ![](p3-sol-fig1)
$\mathrm{S_N2}$ — Bimolecular Nucleophilic Substitution.

$$
\text{Rate}=k[\text{substrate}][\text{nucleophile}].
$$

The overall rate is directly dependent on the concentration of **both** the substrate and the nucleophile. Thus tripling the concentration of both of the reactants will result in a 9-fold increase in the overall reaction rate.
![](p3-sol-fig2)
![](p3-sol-fig3)

figures.alt: Products from two and one equivalents of base
Oxidative coupled product, including lone pairs

problems.title: Problem 4
problems.statement:
Graph paper is provided for your optional use in this question. If you choose to use it, print your name and identification code in the upper right corner of the graph paper.

HIn is a weakly acidic indicator.

$$
\mathrm{HIn+Na^+OH^-\rightleftharpoons Na^+In^-+H_2O},
$$

also written as

$$
\mathrm{HIn\rightleftharpoons In^-+H^+}.
$$

At normal temperatures, the acid dissociation constant is $K_a=2.93\times10^{-5}$. Absorbance data (1.00 cm cells) for $5.00\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{M}$ ($\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$) solutions in strongly acidic and strongly alkaline solutions follow.

| $\lambda$, nm | pH = 1.00 | pH = 13.00 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 400 | 0.401 | 0.067 |
| 470 | 0.447 | 0.050 |
| 485 | 0.453 | 0.052 |
| 490 | 0.452 | 0.054 |
| 505 | 0.443 | 0.073 |
| 535 | 0.390 | 0.170 |
| 555 | 0.342 | 0.342 |
| 570 | 0.303 | 0.515 |
| 585 | 0.263 | 0.648 |
| 615 | 0.195 | 0.816 |
| 625 | 0.176 | 0.823 |
| 635 | 0.170 | 0.816 |
| 650 | 0.137 | 0.763 |
| 680 | 0.097 | 0.588 |

![](p4-fig1)

parts.statement:
Predict the observed colour of the a) acidic and b) basic forms of the indicator. Using a “50 nm wide bar”, shade the appropriate area of the wavelength scale on the answer sheet which would correspond to the colour of the indicator at the pH values given in the table.

For example, if the observed colour is green, your answer would appear as:

![](p4-fig2)
A filter is located between the light source and the sample. What colour filter would be most suitable for the photometric analysis of the indicator in a strongly acidic medium?
What wavelength range would be most suitable for the photometric analysis of the indicator in a strongly basic medium?
What would be the absorbance of a $1.00\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{M}$ ($\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$) solution of the indicator in alkaline form if measured at 545 nm in a 2.50 cm cell?

Solutions were prepared in a strongly acidic solution (HCl, pH = 1) and a strongly basic solution (NaOH, pH = 13). Perfectly linear relationships between absorbance and concentration were observed in both media at 490 nm and 625 nm, respectively. The molar absorptivities are:

| Form | $\lambda=490\ \mathrm{nm}$ | $\lambda=625\ \mathrm{nm}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HIn (HCl) | $9.04\times10^2\ \mathrm{M^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$ | $3.52\times10^2\ \mathrm{M^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$ |
| In⁻ (NaOH) | $1.08\times10^2\ \mathrm{M^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$ | $1.65\times10^3\ \mathrm{M^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$ |

$\mathrm{M=mol\,dm^{-3}}$. Calculate the absorbance (1.00 cm cell) at the two wavelengths for an aqueous $1.80\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{M}$ ($\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$) solution of HIn.

sections.statement:
The observed colour will be complementary to that of the absorption maximum.

a) Acidic conditions (pH 1): the sample absorbs at $490\pm25\ \mathrm{nm}$ (blue-green), transmits the complementary colour, and appears yellow-orange ($625\pm25\ \mathrm{nm}$).

b) Basic conditions (pH 13): it absorbs at $625\pm25\ \mathrm{nm}$ (yellow-orange), transmits the complementary colour, and appears blue-green ($490\pm25\ \mathrm{nm}$).

The filter should transmit the colour the sample absorbs most efficiently. The acidic sample absorbs most strongly in the blue range ($490\pm25\ \mathrm{nm}$), so a similar colour filter is most suitable.
Maximum sensitivity requires the wavelength at which the sample absorbs most strongly. The basic form has maximum absorbance at $625\pm25\ \mathrm{nm}$, the most suitable wavelength range.

A graph of absorbance against wavelength gives 0.256 at 545 nm for a $5.00\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{M}$ basic solution. This region is linear, so the value can also be interpolated from the table.

$$
A=\varepsilon lc,\qquad
\varepsilon=\frac{A}{lc}
=\frac{0.256}{1.0\times5.00\times10^{-4}}
=5.12\times10^2\ \mathrm{M^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}.
$$

Here $l$ is cell length, $c$ analyte concentration and $\varepsilon$ molar absorptivity. For a $1.00\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{M}$ basic solution in a 2.50 cm cell:

$$
A=5.12\times10^2\times2.50\times1.0\times10^{-4}=0.128.
$$

The key prints the “dissociation reaction” as $[\mathrm{HIn}]=[\mathrm{H^+}]+[\mathrm{In^-}]$. It then gives:

$$
[\mathrm{H^+}]=[\mathrm{In^-}]\quad(1),\qquad
[\mathrm{HIn}]+[\mathrm{In^-}]=1.80\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{M}\quad(2),
$$

$$
K_a=\frac{[\mathrm{H^+}][\mathrm{In^-}]}{[\mathrm{HIn}]}\quad(3).
$$

Substituting (1) and (2) into (3):

$$
K_a=\frac{[\mathrm{In^-}]^2}{1.8\times10^{-3}-[\mathrm{In^-}]}
=2.93\times10^{-5}.
$$

Rearrangement gives

$$
[\mathrm{In^-}]^2+2.93\times10^{-5}[\mathrm{In^-}]-5.27\times10^{-8}=0,
$$

and hence

$$
[\mathrm{In^-}]=2.15\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{M},\qquad
[\mathrm{HIn}]=1.80\times10^{-3}-2.15\times10^{-4}
=1.58\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{M}.
$$

The absorbances are:

$$
A_{490}=(9.04\times10^2\times1\times1.58\times10^{-3})
+(1.08\times10^2\times1\times2.15\times10^{-4})=1.45,
$$

$$
A_{625}=(3.52\times10^2\times1\times1.58\times10^{-3})
+(1.65\times10^3\times1\times2.15\times10^{-4})=0.911.
$$

problems.title: Problem 5
problems.statement:
Iron metal melts at 1811 K. Between room temperature and its melting point it can exist in different allotropic or crystalline forms. From room temperature to 1185 K, its body-centred cubic (bcc) lattice is known as $\alpha$-iron. From 1185 K to 1667 K, the structure is face-centred cubic (fcc), called $\gamma$-iron. Above 1667 K to melting it reverts to a bcc structure similar to $\alpha$-iron; this phase is $\delta$-iron.

The density of pure iron is $7.874\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ at 293 K.

parts.statement: Calculate the atomic radius of iron in cm.

Calculate its density in $\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ at 1250 K. Ignore small thermal-expansion effects. Clearly define any symbols used, e.g. $r=$ atomic radius of Fe.

Steel is an iron–carbon alloy in which small carbon atoms occupy some interstitial spaces (“holes”) of the iron crystal lattice. Its carbon content typically ranges from 0.1% to 4.0%. In a blast furnace, melting is facilitated by 4.3% carbon by mass. If this mixture is cooled too rapidly, carbon remains dispersed within the $\alpha$-iron phase. The new solid, martensite, is extremely hard and brittle. Although slightly distorted, its unit-cell size is the same as $\alpha$-iron (bcc).

Assume carbon is evenly distributed in the iron structure.
Calculate the average number of carbon atoms per unit cell of $\alpha$-iron in martensite containing 4.3% C by mass.

Calculate the density of this material in $\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$.

Molar masses and constants:

$$
M(\mathrm{Fe})=55.847\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}},\quad
M(\mathrm{C})=12.011\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}},\quad
N_A=6.02214\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}.
$$

sections.statement:
**Expected steps of the calculation**

1. Define lengths $a,b,c,d_1,d_2,r$ and volumes $V_1,V_2$ for bcc and fcc iron (details below).
2. Calculate $V_1$ of the $\alpha$-iron unit cell from density $\rho_{\mathrm{bcc}}$ at 293 K, molar weight $M(\mathrm{Fe})$, and $N_A$.
3. Calculate bcc edge $d_1$ from $V_1$.
4. Calculate atomic radius $r$ from $d_1$.
5. Calculate fcc edge $d_2$ at 1250 K from $r$.
6. Calculate fcc volume $V_2$ of $\gamma$-iron from $d_2$.
7. Calculate mass $m$ of the iron atoms in a $\gamma$-iron unit cell using $M(\mathrm{Fe})$ and $N_A$.
8. Calculate $\rho_{\mathrm{fcc}}$ from $m$ and $V_2$.

An alternative route uses the percent space-filling ratios of both cells, replacing steps 5–8:

5′. Calculate the bcc space-filling ratio.

6′. Calculate the fcc space-filling ratio.

7′. Calculate $\rho_{\mathrm{fcc}}/\rho_{\mathrm{bcc}}$ from fcc/bcc space-filling ratios.

8′. Calculate $\rho_{\mathrm{fcc}}$ from step 7′.

![](p5-sol-fig1)

![](p5-sol-fig2)

**Calculations in detail**

At 293 K, $\alpha$-iron is bcc: each unit cell has two atoms, one at its centre. At 1250 K, $\gamma$-iron is fcc: each unit cell has four atoms, each side having one-half an atom at its centre.

| Symbol | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| $r$ | atomic radius of iron |
| $a$ | diagonal on one side of the bcc unit cell |
| $b$ | diagonal passing through the centre of the bcc unit cell |
| $c$ | diagonal on one side of the fcc unit cell |
| $d_1$ | edge of the bcc $\alpha$-iron cell |
| $d_2$ | edge of the fcc $\gamma$-iron cell |
| $V_1$ | bcc $\alpha$-iron cell volume |
| $V_2$ | fcc $\gamma$-iron cell volume |
| $V_a$ | volume of one atom |
| $V_{a1}$ | volume occupied by two atoms in a bcc cell |
| $V_{a2}$ | volume occupied by four atoms in an fcc cell |
| $R_1$ | bcc percent space-filling ratio |
| $R_2$ | fcc percent space-filling ratio |

$$
V_a=\frac43\pi r^3,\quad V_{a1}=2V_a,\quad V_{a2}=4V_a.
$$

$$
b=4r,\quad a^2=2d_1^2,\quad b^2=d_1^2+a^2=3d_1^2,
$$

$$
d_1=(b^2/3)^{1/2}=(16r^2/3)^{1/2},\quad
V_1=d_1^3=[(16r^2/3)^{1/2}]^3,
$$

$$
c=4r,\quad c^2=2d_2^2,\quad
d_2=(c^2/2)^{1/2}=(16r^2/2)^{1/2},\quad
V_2=d_2^3=[(16r^2/2)^{1/2}]^3.
$$

2. At 293 K, $1.000\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of iron weighs 7.874 g; a mole weighs 55.847 g. Thus $7.874/55.847=0.1410$ mol occupies $1.000\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, or a mole occupies $7.093\ \mathrm{cm^3}$. A mole corresponds to $6.02214\times10^{23}$ atoms:

$$
V_1=\frac{(7.093\ \mathrm{cm^3\,mol^{-1}})(2\ \text{atoms/unit cell})}
{6.02214\times10^{23}\ \text{atoms/mol}}
=2.356\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3/unit\ cell}.
$$

3. $d_1=V_1^{1/3}=(2.356\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3})^{1/3}=2.867\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}$.

4. For bcc, $d_1=(16r^2/3)^{1/2}$, hence

$$
r=(3d_1^2/16)^{1/2}
=[3(2.867\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm})^2/16]^{1/2}
=1.241\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}.
$$

5. For fcc at 1250 K:

$$
d_2=(16r^2/2)^{1/2}
=[16(1.241\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm})^2/2]^{1/2}
=3.511\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}.
$$

6. $V_2=d_2^3=(3.511\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm})^3=4.327\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.

7. The mass of four iron atoms is

$$
m=\frac{(55.847\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}})(4\ \text{atoms/unit cell})}
{6.02214\times10^{23}\ \text{atoms/mol}}
=3.709\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{g/unit\ cell}.
$$

8. $\rho_{\mathrm{fcc}}=m/V_2=(3.709\times10^{-22})/(4.327\times10^{-23})=8.572\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$.

**Alternative route**

$$
\begin{aligned}
R_1&=\frac{V_{a1}}{V_1}\times100\%
=\frac{2V_a}{V_1}\times100\%\\
&=\frac{2(4/3)\pi r^3}{[(16r^2/3)^{1/2}]^3}\times100\%
=\frac{(8/3)\pi r^3}{(16/3)^{3/2}r^3}\times100\%\\
&=\frac{(8/3)\pi}{(16/3)^{3/2}}\times100\%
=\frac{8.378}{12.32}\times100\%=68.02\%.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
R_2&=\frac{V_{a2}}{V_2}\times100\%
=\frac{4V_a}{V_2}\times100\%\\
&=\frac{4(4/3)\pi r^3}{[(16r^2/2)^{1/2}]^3}\times100\%
=\frac{(16/3)\pi r^3}{8^{3/2}r^3}\times100\%\\
&=\frac{(16/3)\pi}{8^{3/2}}\times100\%
=\frac{16.76}{22.63}\times100\%=74.05\%.
\end{aligned}
$$

7′. $\rho_{\mathrm{fcc}}/\rho_{\mathrm{bcc}}=74.05\%/68.02\%=1.089$.

8′. $\rho_{\mathrm{fcc}}=1.089\rho_{\mathrm{bcc}}=1.089\times7.874=8.572\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$.

**Expected steps**

1. From martensite's mass-percent composition calculate relative moles of C and Fe.
2. Bring the C/Fe molar ratio to one unit cell (two Fe atoms).
3. Find the smallest whole number of C atoms for the smallest whole number of unit cells (facultative).
4. Calculate iron mass per cell.
5. Calculate carbon mass per cell.
6. Calculate total C and Fe mass in one cell.
7. Calculate martensite density from total C and Fe mass and bcc volume $V_1$.

**Details**

1. In 100.0 g of 4.3% C martensite:

$$
\frac{4.3\ \mathrm{g\ C}}{12.011\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}}=0.36\ \mathrm{mol\ C},\quad
\frac{95.7\ \mathrm{g\ Fe}}{55.847\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}}=1.71\ \mathrm{mol\ Fe}.
$$

There is one carbon atom for 4.8 iron atoms, or 0.21 carbon atoms per iron atom.

2. Martensite is bcc with two iron atoms per cell:

$$
\frac{1\ \mathrm{C\ atom}}{4.8\ \mathrm{Fe\ atoms}}\,
\frac{2\ \mathrm{Fe\ atoms}}{\mathrm{unit\ cell}}
=0.42\ \mathrm{C\ atoms/unit\ cell}.
$$

3. Five carbon atoms $[(0.42\ \mathrm{C\ atom}/0.42)\times5]$ in 12 cells $[(1\ \mathrm{unit\ cell}/0.42)\times5]$: five carbon atoms dispersed in 12 unit cells.

4. Iron mass per $\alpha$-iron cell:

$$
\frac{55.847\ \mathrm{g/mol}}{6.02214\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{atoms/mol}}\,
\frac{2\ \mathrm{atoms}}{\mathrm{unit\ cell}}
=1.8547\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{g\ Fe/unit\ cell}.
$$

5. Carbon mass per atom is $12.011/(6.02214\times10^{23})=1.9945\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{g\ C/atom}$.

6. Total cell mass:

$$
1.8547\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{g\ Fe}
+(0.42\ \mathrm{C\ atoms})(1.9945\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{g/C\ atom})
=1.938\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{g\ C\ and\ Fe}.
$$

7. Each cell occupies $V_1=2.356\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ (“cf. Question i”):

$$
\rho(\text{martensite at }4.3\%\mathrm{\ C})
=\frac{1.938\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{g\ C\ and\ Fe}}
{2.356\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}}
=8.228\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}.
$$

problems.title: Problem 6

sections.statement:
Much of the world's platinum-group metal supply is derived from residues recovered from electrolytic refining of copper and nickel. A recovery flow chart for platinum and palladium follows.

![](p6-fig1)

parts.label: i
parts.statement: Clearly draw the shape (geometry) of both $\mathrm{PtCl_6^{2-}}$ and $\mathrm{PdCl_4^{2-}}$.

parts.label: ii
parts.statement: Clearly draw all possible stereoisomeric structures of monomeric $\mathrm{Pd(NH_3)_2Cl_2}$. Label them with the correct stereochemical descriptors.

parts.label: iii
parts.statement: What is the role of $\mathrm{FeSO_4}$ in the second step of the flow chart? Write a balanced equation for its reaction in this step.

parts.label: iv
parts.statement: Write a complete balanced equation for ignition of $\mathrm{Pd(NH_3)_2Cl_2}$ in air to give Pd metal. What is oxidized and what is reduced?

sections.statement:
Reaction of a main-group chloride (24.71 g) with ammonia (10.90 g) gave $\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$ (25.68 g), a solid element **A** (2.57 g), and a yellow crystalline nitride of **A** (7.37 g), according to

$$
n\mathrm{A}_w\mathrm{Cl}_x+m\mathrm{NH_3}
\longrightarrow p\mathrm{NH_4Cl}+q\mathrm{A}+r\mathrm{A}_y\mathrm{N}_z.
$$

The coefficients $n,m,p,q,r,w,x,y,z$ are to be determined. A nitride sample exploded violently when struck with a hammer but underwent controlled polymerization on heating to a bronze-coloured fibrous solid exhibiting metallic conductivity. **A** also polymerizes to a high-molecular-weight linear polymer on heating.

Molar masses: $M(\mathrm{Cl})=35.453$, $M(\mathrm{N})=14.007$, $M(\mathrm{H})=1.008\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$.

parts.label: i
parts.statement: Identify element **A**.

parts.label: ii
parts.statement: Write a complete balanced equation for the reaction of the chloride with ammonia.

parts.label: iii
parts.statement: Assuming conventional oxidation states, write the balanced redox half-reaction equations involved.

sections.statement:
### i

$\mathrm{PtCl_6^{2-}}$ consists of Pt(IV) centred in a regular octahedron of Cl⁻ ions. The printed prose describes $\mathrm{PdCl_4^{2-}}$ as “Pt(II)” centred in a square of Cl⁻ ions; the native diagram labels its centre Pd.

![](p6-sol-fig1)

### ii

Like $\mathrm{PdCl_4^{2-}}$, $\mathrm{Pd(NH_3)_2Cl_2}$ is square planar. There are two arrangements of the two ligand types. Placing both Cl⁻ ions on adjacent corners (and both NH₃ on the other adjacent corners) gives the *cis* isomer. Placing like ligand pairs on diagonally opposite corners gives the *trans* isomer. Only these two stereoisomers are possible for the monomeric complex.

![](p6-sol-fig2)

### iii

$\mathrm{FeSO_4}$, i.e. Fe(II), is a reducing agent. Under the process conditions it reduces Au(III) to Au(0), but is not strong enough to reduce Pd(II) or Pt(IV).

$$
\mathrm{HAuCl_4+3FeSO_4\longrightarrow Au^0+HCl+FeCl_3+Fe_2(SO_4)_3}.
$$

### iv

The key prints three alternative ignition equations and their half-reactions:

$$
\mathrm{Pd(NH_3)_2Cl_2+O_2\longrightarrow Pd^0+N_2+2H_2O+2HCl}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Pd^{2+}+2e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{Pd^0}&&\text{reduction},\\
\mathrm{2O^0+4e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{2O^{2-}}&&\text{reduction},\\
\mathrm{2N^{3-}-6e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{2N^0}&&\text{oxidation}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Or:

$$
\mathrm{Pd(NH_3)_2Cl_2+2O_2\longrightarrow Pd^0+2NO+2H_2O+2HCl},
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Pd^{2+}+2e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{Pd^0}&&\text{reduction},\\
\mathrm{4O^0+8e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{4O^{2-}}&&\text{reduction},\\
\mathrm{2N^{3-}-10e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{2N^{2+}}&&\text{oxidation}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Or:

$$
\mathrm{Pd(NH_3)_2Cl_2+3O_2\longrightarrow Pd^0+2NO_2+2H_2O+2HCl},
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Pd^{2+}+2e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{Pd^0}&&\text{reduction},\\
\mathrm{6O^0+12e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{6O^{2-}}&&\text{reduction},\\
\mathrm{2N^{3-}-14e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{2N^{4+}}&&\text{oxidation}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Ammonia is oxidized to water and dinitrogen (or nitrogen oxides); Pd(II) and dioxygen are reduced. Part of the oxidation supplies two electrons to convert Pd(II) to Pd(0), and part reduces dioxygen to water. Noble-metal catalysts can oxidize NH₃ to $(\mathrm{NO})_x$, so other nitrogen species are possible in principle.

### i

**A = sulphur.**

All chlorine is in NH₄Cl. Since 53.492 g NH₄Cl contains 35.453 g Cl, 25.68 g NH₄Cl contains

$$
25.68\times35.453/53.492=17.02\ \mathrm{g\ Cl}.
$$

The printed total amount of A is “24.71 g Cl − 17.02 g Cl = 7.69 g A”. There are 2.57 g free A and $7.69-2.57=5.12$ g A in the nitride. Nitride nitrogen is $7.37-5.12=2.25$ g. The key also prints “nitrogen bound in NH₄Cl” as $25.68-17.02=8.66$ g.

Apply the rule of multiple proportions.

**Proportions 1:1**

Chloride: 7.69 g A binds 17.02 g Cl. The amount binding 35.453 g Cl is

$$
35.453\times7.69/17.02=16.02\ \mathrm{g}.
$$

A could be oxygen, but it is a gas and is excluded.

Nitride: 5.12 g A binds 2.25 g N. The amount binding 14.007 g N is

$$
14.007\times5.12/2.25=31.87\ \mathrm{g}.
$$

Sulphur fits the physical description and $M_r(\mathrm{S})=32.064$. The key's footnote states that phosphorus, $M_r(\mathrm{P})=30.97$, is also possible but must be excluded because the highest known degree of “polymerization” is four, in P₄.

**Proportions 1:2**

Chloride: 7.69 g A binds 17.02 g Cl. The amount binding $2\times35.453$ g Cl is

$$
2\times35.453\times7.69/17.02=32.03\ \mathrm{g}.
$$

Again sulphur is possible.

Nitride: 5.12 g A binds 2.25 g N. The amount binding $2\times14.007$ g N is

$$
2\times14.007\times5.12/2.25=63.75\ \mathrm{g}.
$$

Cu is possible numerically but is a Group B element and is excluded. Therefore A is sulphur.

### ii

$$
\mathrm{3SCl_2+8NH_3\longrightarrow6NH_4Cl+S+S_2N_2},
$$

or

$$
\mathrm{6SCl_2+16NH_3\longrightarrow12NH_4Cl+2S+S_4N_4}.
$$

The native key says elemental S is S₈ and therefore the equation should be multiplied by eight. Although S₂N₂ roughly fits the colour and explosive instability, S₄N₄ is actually produced. Carefully controlled heating polymerizes both rings to the high-molecular-weight linear polymer $(\mathrm{SN})_n$, one of the rare examples of a metal containing only lighter p-group elements.

Polymerization is favoured by relatively weak S–N bonds and large ring strain. The weak S–S bond is also broken by heating, so S₈ polymerizes at high temperature. S₈ has hardly any ring-strain energy, so its polymerization is not highly exothermic or explosive. Other sulphur chlorides, S₂Cl₂ and SCl₄, do not fit the reaction stoichiometry.

### iii

Sulphur disproportionation:

$$
\mathrm{2S^{2+}-2e^-\longrightarrow2S^{3+}},\qquad
\mathrm{S^{2+}+2e^-\longrightarrow S^0}.
$$

problems.title: Problem 7

sections.statement:
One mole of ideal $\mathrm{Cl_2(g)}$, initially at 300 K and $1.01325\times10^7\ \mathrm{Pa}$, expands against constant external pressure $1.01325\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$ to this same final pressure. It cools to 239 K (the normal boiling point), and 0.100 mol of Cl₂ condenses.

At the normal boiling point, $\Delta H_{\mathrm{vap}}=20.42\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, $C_v(\mathrm{Cl_2(g)})=28.66\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$, and liquid density is $1.56\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. Assume $C_p=C_v+R$.

$$
1\ \mathrm{atm}=1.01325\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa},\qquad
R=8.314510\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}
=0.0820584\ \mathrm{L\,atm\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}.
$$

parts.label: i
parts.statement: Either draw a complete molecular-orbital energy diagram or write the complete electronic configuration of Cl₂. Predict the bond order and whether the molecule is diamagnetic, ferromagnetic or paramagnetic.

parts.label: ii
parts.statement: Calculate the changes in internal energy $\Delta E$ and system entropy $\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}}$ for the changes above.

sections.statement:
The following reactions occur in dilute aqueous solution at 298 K:

$$
\mathrm{[Ni(H_2O)_6]^{2+}+2NH_3
\rightleftharpoons[Ni(NH_3)_2(H_2O)_4]^{2+}+2H_2O}\quad(1)
$$

with $\ln K_c=11.60$, $\Delta H^0=-33.5\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, and

$$
\mathrm{[Ni(H_2O)_6]^{2+}+en
\rightleftharpoons[Ni(en)(H_2O)_4]^{2+}+2H_2O}\quad(2)
$$

with $\ln K_c=17.78$, $\Delta H^0=-37.2\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Here en is ethylenediamine, a neutral bidentate ligand. Use the gas constant given above.

Calculate $\Delta G^0$, $\Delta S^0$ and $K_c$ at 298 K for

$$
\mathrm{[Ni(NH_3)_2(H_2O)_4]^{2+}+en
\rightleftharpoons[Ni(en)(H_2O)_4]^{2+}+2NH_3}\quad(3).
$$

### i

Cl atomic configuration:

$$
1s^2\,2s^2\,2p_x^2\,2p_y^2\,2p_z^2\,3s^2\,3p_x^2\,3p_y^2\,3p_z^1.
$$

Significant atomic orbitals (AO): $1(K)+4(L)+4(M)=9$, containing 17 electrons. The number of molecular orbitals equals the number of AOs, so $2[1(K)+4(L)+4(M)]=18$ MOs in Cl₂, containing $2\times17=34$ electrons.

![](p7-sol-fig1)

The key prints all four alternative configurations:

$$
(1\sigma)^2(1\sigma^*)^2(2\sigma)^2(2\sigma^*)^2(3\sigma)^2
(1\pi)^4(1\pi^*)^4(3\sigma^*)^2(4\sigma)^2(4\sigma^*)^2
(5\sigma)^2(2\pi)^4(2\pi^*)^4;
$$

or

$$
(KK)(LL)(\sigma3s)^2(\sigma^*3s)^2(\sigma3p)^2
(\pi3p)^4(\pi^*3p)^4;
$$

or

$$
\begin{aligned}
&(\sigma1s)^2(\sigma^*1s)^2(\sigma2s)^2(\sigma^*2s)^2
(\sigma2p_z)^2(\pi2p_x)^2(\pi2p_y)^2
(\pi^*2p_x)^2(\pi^*2p_y)^2(\sigma^*2p_z)^2\\
&\qquad(\sigma3s)^2(\sigma^*3s)^2(\sigma3p_z)^2
(\pi3p_x)^2(\pi3p_y)^2(\pi^*3p_x)^2(\pi^*3p_y)^2
(\sigma^*2p_z)^0;
\end{aligned}
$$

or

$$
(KK)(LL)(\sigma3s)^2(\sigma^*3s)^2(\sigma3p_z)^2
(\pi3p_x)^2(\pi3p_y)^2(\pi^*3p_x)^2(\pi^*3p_y)^2
(\sigma^*2p_z)^0.
$$

Assumption: bonding along the $z$-axis; equivalent formulae for $x$ or $y$ are accepted. The last unoccupied orbital is printed with **2**$p_z$ in the last two formulae, retained here.

Bond order is $(n-n^*)/2$ with $n=18$, $n^*=16$: $(18-16)/2=1$ (one σ bond, no π bond). Cl₂ is diamagnetic because there are no unpaired electrons.

### ii

![](p7-sol-fig2)

Expansion plus an isobaric gas-to-liquid phase change forms the total process. Internal energy is a state function, so $\Delta E=\Delta E_1+\Delta E_2$.

**Process 1**

The native arithmetic line is retained:

$$
\Delta E_1=\int nC_v\,dT
=1\times28.66\times239-300=-1748.3\ \mathrm{J}.
$$

Notes: a) perfect-gas $\Delta E$ depends only on $T$; b) $C_v$ is constant; c) the minus sign indicates loss of energy due to expansion work on one mole of gas.

**Process 2**

For convenience the data are manipulated in atm; using Pa requires the appropriate conversion. Liquid formation separates into vaporization heat loss to the surroundings (decreased internal energy; at constant pressure heat equals enthalpy change), and work done by the surroundings compressing the system (increased internal energy).

Gas volume condensed:

$$
V=\frac{nRT}{P}
=\frac{0.1\times0.0820584\times239}{1}
=1.96\ \mathrm{dm^3}.
$$

Liquid volume: $(0.1\times2\times35.454)/1.56=4.54\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.

$$
\Delta E_2=\Delta H_2-\int P_{\mathrm{ext}}\Delta V
=\Delta H_2-P_{\mathrm{ext}}(V_l-V_g).
$$

$V_l$ is approximately zero and is neglected. The native parenthesis reads “ca. 4.5 cm³ liquid volume vs. ca. 17.6 dm³; ca. 0.03% error”.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta E_2&=0.1(-\Delta H_{\mathrm{vap}})+P_{\mathrm{ext}}V_g\\
&=0.1(-20420)+(1\times1.96\ \mathrm{L})
(101.325\ \mathrm{J\,dm^{-3}\,atm^{-1}})\\
&=-2042.0+198.5=-1843.5\ \mathrm{J}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\Delta E=-1748.3+(-1843.5)=-3591.8\ \mathrm{J}.
$$

Entropy is a function of two state variables; in Process 1 known variables are $T,P$, so choose $S(T,P)$.

$$
\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}}=\Delta S_1+\Delta S_2,\quad
C_p=C_v+R=28.66+8.314=36.97\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}},
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta S_1&=nC_p\ln\frac{T_2}{T_1}-nR\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}\\
&=1.0\times36.97\ln\frac{239}{300}
-8.314\ln\frac1{100}\\
&=-8.40+38.29=29.89\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For constant-temperature phase transition $\Delta S_2=Q/T$. At constant pressure $Q/T=Q_p/T=\Delta H/T$:

$$
\Delta S_2=\frac{0.1(-20420)}{239}
=-8.54\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}},\qquad
\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}}=29.89-8.54=21.35\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}.
$$

Beware of round-off errors: conversions into and out of logarithmic relationships can yield small differences. The approach matters. Reversing reaction 1 reverses signs of $\ln K_c$ and $\Delta H^0$. Equilibrium constants multiply when equations add, so $\ln K$ values add.

Reaction $3=2-1$, thus $\Delta S_3=\Delta S_2-\Delta S_1$, $\Delta G_3=\Delta G_2-\Delta G_1$.

$$
\Delta G_1^0=-RT\ln K_{c1}
=-8.314\times298\times11.60
=-28740\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}=-28.74\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}},
$$

$$
\Delta H_1^0=-33.5\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}},\qquad
\Delta S_1^0=\frac{\Delta H_1^0-\Delta G_1^0}{T}
=\frac{-33.5-(-28.74)}{298}
=-0.0161\ \mathrm{kJ\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}
=-16.1\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}.
$$

Similarly, the key prints:

$$
\Delta G_2^0=-44.05\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}},\quad
\Delta H_2^0=-37.2\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}},\quad
\Delta S_2^0=-22.98\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}.
$$

For reaction 3 the printed values are

$$
\Delta H_3^0=\Delta H_2^0-\Delta H_1^0=-3.7\ \mathrm{kJ},\quad
\Delta S_3^0=\Delta S_2^0-\Delta S_1^0=39.08\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}},
$$

$$
\Delta G_3^0=\Delta H_3^0-T\Delta S_3^0=-15.35\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}},\qquad
K_{c3}=e^{15.35/(RT)}=4.90\times10^2.
$$

Alternatively:

$$
\Delta G_3^0=\Delta G_2^0-\Delta G_1^0=-44.05-(-28.74)
=-15.31\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}},\quad K=4.82\times10^2,
$$

$$
\Delta S^0=\frac{\Delta H^0-\Delta G^0}{T}
=\frac{-3700-(-15311)}{298}=38.96\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}.
$$

problems.title: Problem 8
problems.statement:
An electrolyte made from H₂SO₄, CuSO₄ and distilled water has volume $100.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, $c(\mathrm{H^+})=1.000\ \mathrm{M}$ and $c(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}})=1.000\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{M}$ ($\mathrm{M=mol\,dm^{-3}}$). Two cubic single-crystal platinum electrodes are immersed. Only each (100) face is exposed; the other five faces are physically blocked by an insulator stable in the electrolyte. Each exposed area is $1.000\ \mathrm{cm^2}$.

During electrolysis 2.0000 C passes between the electrodes. Epitaxial (layer-by-layer) Cu deposition and H₂ generation occur simultaneously at the cathode; O₂ forms at the anode. The collected H₂ behaves ideally, with $T=273.15\ \mathrm{K}$, $P=1.01325\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}$ and volume $2.0000\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.

parts.statement: Write equations for the electrode processes.
Calculate moles of H₂ generated and Cu deposited at the cathode.

Calculate Cu monolayers formed on the Pt (100) cathode. The Pt lattice constant is $a(\mathrm{Pt})=3.9236\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}$. Both Pt and Cu are fcc.

Constants:

| Quantity | Value |
| --- | --- |
| $M(\mathrm{H})$ | $1.00795\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$ |
| $M(\mathrm{Cu})$ | $63.546\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$ |
| $e$ | $1.60218\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$ |
| $F$ | $96485.3\ \mathrm{C\,mol^{-1}}$ |
| $R$ | $8.314510\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}=0.0820584\ \mathrm{L\,atm\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ |
| $V_m$ | $22.4141\ \mathrm{dm^3}$ |
| 1 atm | $1.01325\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$ |
| $N_A$ | $6.02214\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}$ |

solution.statement:
**Approach**

- Determine H₂ moles.
- Calculate H₂-production charge and Cu-deposition charge, hence Cu moles.
- Calculate Pt (100) surface atom concentration per cm². Epitaxial Cu has the same number of atoms per cm².
- Determine charge for one Cu monolayer, then the monolayer count.

sections.statement:
The anode line is printed as

$$
\mathrm{2H_2O\longrightarrow H^++O_2+4e^-}.
$$

Two simultaneous cathode reactions:

$$
\mathrm{2H^++2e^-\longrightarrow H_2},\qquad
\mathrm{Cu^{2+}+2e^-\longrightarrow Cu}.
$$

For $2.0000\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ H₂ at 273.15 K and 10.1325 kPa, two approaches give its moles.

**Ideal-gas law** $pV=n(\mathrm{H_2})RT$:

$$
n(\mathrm{H_2})
=\frac{10132.5\times2.0000\times10^{-6}}{8.314510\times273.15}
=8.9230\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{mol}.
$$

**Molar volume** $n(\mathrm{H_2})=V(\mathrm{H_2})/V_m$. Here $V_m=22.4141\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}}$ at 1 atm (101.325 kPa). Since H₂ pressure is ten times smaller, its volume at 1 atm would be $0.2000\ \mathrm{cm^3}$:

$$
n(\mathrm{H_2})=\frac{0.20000\times10^{-3}}{22.4141}
=8.9230\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{mol}.
$$

Two charge approaches:

a) H atoms are twice the H₂ molecules; multiplying atom number by $e$ gives charge:

$$
Q_H=2(8.9230\times10^{-6})N_A(1.60218\times10^{-19})
=1.7219\ \mathrm{C}.
$$

b) Faraday's law $m_H=k_HQ_H$, where $k_H$ is H mass generated by 1 C. One faraday, 96485.3 C, gives one mole H (half a mole H₂):

$$
k_H=\frac{1.0000\times1.00795}{96485.3}
=1.04467\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{g\,C^{-1}},
$$

$$
Q_H=\frac{m_H}{k_H}
=\frac{2(8.9230\times10^{-6})(1.00795)}
{1.04467\times10^{-5}}
=1.7219\ \mathrm{C}.
$$

Cu-deposition charge:

$$
Q_{\mathrm{Cu}}=2.0000-Q_H=2.0000-1.7219=0.2781\ \mathrm{C}.
$$

Cu moles: $0.2781/(2F)=1.4412\times10^{-6}$.

Pt (100) fundamental-unit area:

$$
A_u=a_{\mathrm{Pt}}^2=1.5395\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{cm^2}.
$$

Each fundamental (100) unit contains $n_u=2$ atoms. Its surface atom concentration is

$$
\sigma_{\mathrm{Pt}(100)}=\frac{n_u}{A_u}
=\frac2{1.5395\times10^{-15}}
=1.2991\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}}.
$$

Epitaxial growth gives $\sigma_{\mathrm{Cu}(100)}=\sigma_{\mathrm{Pt}(100)}$. One Cu monolayer requires

$$
q_{\mathrm{ML}}=2e(1.2991\times10^{15})
=4.1628\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{C}.
$$

The native final numerator is 0.2780 C:

$$
n_{\mathrm{ML}}=\frac{0.2780\ \mathrm{C}}{4.1628\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{C}}
=668\ \mathrm{ML}.
$$

Alternatively, calculate the $8.6802\times10^{17}$ Cu atoms from deposited moles and divide by $1.2991\times10^{15}$ atoms on the exposed Pt surface: again 668 monolayers.
